paragraph.text: J23. "What would we do with the animals if everyone went vegan?"

no one goes vegan all at once across the whole world. Change is gradual, and with less demand, fewer animals are bred. Farmed animals exist in enormous numbers because they're bred for this (C12). Those who already exist could live in sanctuaries or until the natural end of their lives. And whole economies have already reorganized when an industry built on exploitation came to an end: whaling shrank until it was banned in most of the world, and, in a far graver case, human slavery, which was also an industry, was abolished without economies ceasing to exist. The problem isn't what to do with them; it's that we keep bringing them into the world to die.
"Release the cows into the streets? They'd have to kill them all at once."
There are billions of farmed animals in the world.
Many wouldn't survive if released into the wild.
If everyone stopped eating meat, there'd be nothing to do with them.
So veganism is impractical or would lead to a catastrophe for the animals themselves.
P1 and P2 are true. The problem lies in P3: change would be gradual, and the animals' breeding is controlled by the farmers.
fails because that change doesn't happen.
"They'd have to kill them all at once."
"Who's going to look after billions of animals?"
"Without farming, these animals wouldn't even exist." (which is B7)

People won't all stop eating meat on the same day. It happens little by little. When fewer people buy meat, farms breed fewer animals. The animals that already exist can live until they're old, some in sanctuaries, which are like homes for rescued animals. This has happened before: many cities used to be lit with whale oil, and when other kinds of light came along, that industry faded away, and life went on.

That won't happen, because no one goes vegan all at once across the whole world: change is gradual. With less demand, farmers breed fewer animals, because breeding is controlled through insemination and hatcheries. The animals that exist can live out their lives, some in sanctuaries. There wouldn't be cows loose in your street; there'd be fewer cows being born to die. And whole industries have ended without catastrophe: whaling was replaced by kerosene and later banned, and even human slavery, which was also an industry, was abolished, and economies reorganized. The question isn't what to do with them, but why keep bringing them into the world only to die.
"If hatcheries incubate eggs according to demand, what happens when demand falls?"
The argument imagines a scenario that doesn't happen:
Everyone stops eating meat at once
Billions of animals are left with nowhere to go
Fewer animals are bred each year
The animals would have to be released or killed
Existing ones live out their lives; new ones stop being born
Industries built on exploitation have ended, and economies reorganized
Meat consumption shifts over years and generations.
Chickens hatch in hatcheries and cattle and pigs are born through insemination, in numbers set by demand (C12).
In sanctuaries, on small holdings or to the end of their cycle, while breeding declines.
The problem isn't what to do with the animals if we stop eating them; it's that we keep breeding billions of them to die.
Many production breeds have health problems caused by breeding (B8). Breeding fewer of them is no loss to the animals.

text.bold: 6. Whole industries have ended, and economies reorganized.

paragraph.text: Whaling is a close example. In the 19th century, whale oil lit homes and cities, and the whaling fleet of New Bedford, in the United States, reached 329 ships in 1856. After the first commercial oil well was drilled in 1859, kerosene became cheaper, and the whaling industry gradually became obsolete, along with its investments, its know-how and its workers. In the 20th century, the International Whaling Commission adopted a moratorium on commercial whaling in 1982, in force since 1986, and Brazil banned the hunting of cetaceans in 1987. A few countries still hunt whales, but the industry that once lit the world disappeared without economic catastrophe.

text.bold: 7. Even human slavery, which was also an industry, was abolished.

paragraph.text: For centuries, the labor of enslaved people sustained the sugar plantations of the British Caribbean and the sugar and coffee plantations of Brazil. Britain abolished slavery in most of its colonies in 1833, and Brazil did so in 1888, with the Golden Law. The economies went through crises and changes, but reorganized around free labor. The comparison is limited and holds for one point only: the economic transition of a whole industry is possible. It doesn't equate the victims or diminish what was specific about slavery. And it also shows what not to do: Britain paid 20 million pounds to the slave-owners, about 40% of public spending in 1833, and forced the freed people into years of unpaid "apprenticeship", while Brazil's Golden Law, just two articles long, gave the freed people no land, no education and no support at all, with consequences that last to this day. A just transition takes care of those who were exploited, not only of those who exploited them.
Farmed animals make up about 60% of mammal biomass

(d) The strongest counter-reply: some breeds would disappear
The most serious version points out that, with the end of farming, many domestic breeds could disappear, and that this would be a loss of diversity.
(e) Why the counter-reply doesn't reach the conclusion
What matters morally is the animals who feel, not the continuity of a breed (A10).

text.bold: Many breeds suffer because of selection.

paragraph.text: Chickens who can barely walk lose nothing by not being born.

The question about the animals' fate is legitimate, but the answer is simple: stop breeding them for slaughter. History shows that whole industries built on exploitation can end, and that what matters is making the transition with care for the victims. The moral problem isn't what to do with them afterwards; it's continuing to bring them into the world to die.

paragraph.text: Many domestic breeds have already disappeared.
An imaginary scenario excuses real change
The current number of animals seems natural
The principle being tested is: "if we stop using something, we'd have to destroy what already exists".
Ending breeding would require killing existing dogs
Banning carts would require killing the horses
The end of the whaling industry would have ruined economies
Ending consumption would require killing them
The question about the fate of existing animals is legitimate, and a responsible transition needs to answer it, with sanctuaries, public policy and care for the animals already alive.
But the scenario of billions of animals set loose doesn't happen, because change is gradual and breeding is controlled. The best way to care for farmed animals is to stop breeding them to die.
